name: Hypothesis Testing
description: True or false statements on p-values, error types, power and the misreadings that surround them.

questions.question: The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the observed data.
questions.explain: It is the reverse conditional: the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null is true. The probability that a hypothesis is true is a Bayesian quantity that a frequentist p-value does not provide.

questions.question: The p-value is computed under the assumption that the null hypothesis holds.
questions.explain: The null distribution is what the test statistic is compared against, so the entire calculation is conditional on H₀. This is exactly why the p-value cannot then be read as a probability about H₀ itself.

questions.question: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not the same as demonstrating that the null hypothesis is true.
questions.explain: A non-significant result can equally mean the effect is real but the study lacked power to detect it. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; establishing practical equivalence requires a different test design.

questions.question: Lowering the significance level from 0.05 to 0.01 reduces the chance of a Type I error but, with everything else held fixed, increases the chance of a Type II error.
questions.explain: A stricter threshold makes rejection harder, so false positives fall and false negatives rise. The only way to improve both at once is to increase the sample size or reduce measurement noise.

questions.question: A Type I error occurs when a test fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false.
questions.explain: That describes a Type II error. A Type I error is rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true, and its long-run rate is the significance level α.

questions.question: With a sample of 50,000 observations, a result significant at α = 0.05 necessarily indicates an effect large enough to matter in practice.
questions.explain: Large samples make even trivially small effects statistically detectable, so significance says nothing about magnitude. Effect sizes and confidence intervals, not p-values, are what answer the practical question.

questions.question: The power of a test is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is in fact true.
questions.explain: Power equals 1 − β, the complement of the Type II error rate. It is defined against a specific alternative effect size, so quoting power without stating that effect size is meaningless.

questions.question: Increasing the sample size while keeping α fixed raises both the power of the test and the probability of a Type I error.
questions.explain: Power does rise with sample size, but the Type I error rate is fixed by the analyst at α and does not depend on n. The subtle trap is that the first half of the statement is correct.

questions.question: For a standard two-sided test, a 95% confidence interval that excludes the null value corresponds to a p-value below 0.05.
questions.explain: The interval contains exactly the null values that would not be rejected at α = 0.05, so exclusion and rejection agree. This duality is why reporting the interval is generally more informative than reporting the p-value alone.

questions.question: Choosing the significance level after inspecting the data, so that the threshold suits the observed result, keeps the test valid as long as the level is stated in the report.
questions.explain: Setting α after seeing the data inflates the true false-positive rate far above the nominal level, whether or not it is disclosed. The threshold and the hypotheses have to be fixed before the data are examined.
